Defining scope

When defining the project scope, early identification of client objectives helps to translate the requirements for EY’s services. The requirements and associated quality criteria may come from a variety of sources including:

  • Operational needs or changes
  • Industry standards, laws and regulations
  • Technical specifications
  • Professional standards
  • Stakeholder requirements

The starting point for project is scope definition. Scope, in practical terms, is more than just the list of items the project will deliver. It also includes other details concerning the timeline and cost. Therefore, scoping an project results in understanding the client’s needs with enough detail to identify:

  • Background information — why this initiative, why now?
  • Objectives — what is the client trying to achieve?
  • Work products — what output will the activities of the project produce?
    EY’s service(s) and the project approach
    Preliminary timeline and economics — about how long and how much?
  • Assumptions — pre-conditions or working hypothesis
  • Constraints — limitations, restrictions
  • Risks — what could go wrong?
  • Quality — how will we know when we have met the client’s quality criteria/standards?

Scope definition considers factors that affect service delivery and economics such as:

  • Organizational scope — how many of the client’s business units or departments are involved?
  • Logical scope — what components of the business process are in/out of scope?
  • Temporal scope — what is the expected duration/timeline?
  • Technical scope — what components of a system or IT infrastructure are involved?
  • Geographical scope — how many locations are involved?

Beyond these factors, defining scope requires:

  • Defining in and out of scope
  • Considering quality management
  • Considering benefit and change management
  • Understanding variances and contingency
  • Understanding sources of variance

Defining in and out of scope

Understanding the factors noted above provides a framework for definition of the project outcome in terms of expected overall results along with the supporting services, work products, or reports necessary to meet the client’s requirements. Documenting (writing a description of) each output is a major element of defining scope. The descriptions serve as a starting point for defining the project plan, and client project charter that will be needed throughout the project. Defining in scope also has the effect of clarifying what is out of scope; although in early planning there may be uncertainties.

As planning progresses, the Project Team must confirm what is in and out of scope by:

  • Obtaining additional information; refining scope detail
  • Identifying risks
  • Defining quality acceptance criteria
  • Defining completion criteria
  • Identifying assumptions and constraints
  • Identifying areas of uncertainty that require additional research or planning allowances (such as stating a range of values — 15-20 interviews — rather than a specific number)

Collectively, these dimensions form the boundary between what is in or out of scope of the project. In scope includes details such as the definitions of activities and work products aligned with the desired project outcome. Out of scope defines items over and above in scope. Assumptions and constraints are used to document out of scope by defining limitations relative to the project scope definition. Examples:

  • The scope of project will include the Finance departments, but will not include other departments
  • The scope of project will assess only the accounts payable process, not accounts receivable, capital management or other financial processes
  • The scope of project will assess the headquarters location, but not any remote sites

Defining the service delivery approach

Documenting the service delivery approach and work products are critical elements of defining scope. Clear definitions serve as a starting point for defining the baseline project plan and Client Project Charter that will guide the Execute phase of the project.

Project scope can cover various aspects. It can be organizational (targeting certain client business units or departments), logical (addressing certain business processes), temporal (defining the timeline or projected duration), technical (addressing system components or IT infrastructure) and geographical (stating the applicable locations). Understanding what is in scope will clarify what is out of scope.

In the early stages of planning, uncertainty may exist about the appropriate approach or what exactly is in or out of scope. As planning progresses, these uncertainties are addressed by:

  • Following the service delivery guidance
  • Obtaining additional detail concerning the content of the work products
  • Refining scope detail
  • Estimating the work required
  • Identifying risks
  • Identifying quality criteria
  • Documenting assumptions and constraints
  • Additionally, details of timing, resources, costs, and other factors define the overall service delivery approach.

Team members should continue to work with the client and others to gather information on project scope to refine the WBS and adjust the project schedule, cost estimate, resource requirements and risks.
